protections: Refuse to build or issue a request when an interpolated lng/ns value could restructure the request URL: a per-key URL-segment denylist (isSafeUrlSegmentBase + strict lng / loose ns helpers, routed by SAFETY_CHECK_BY_KEY) is applied by interpolateUrl to every placeholder before loadPath/addPath templates are handed to options.request (lib/utils.js:26-75, lib/utils.js:147-165, lib/index.js:64, lib/index.js:133). The same guard is duplicated in the checked-in browser bundles (i18nextHttpBackend.js:11-28, i18nextHttpBackend.js:76-92, i18nextHttpBackend.min.js:1).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: The shared denylist's own comment enumerates the URL-structure characters it blocks as `?`, `#`, `%` and whitespace (lib/utils.js:32-35), so the check reads as a complete answer to 'URL-structure injection'; nothing in the function says the scheme delimiter `:` is also structural when a template begins with the placeholder.

The ns helper is deliberately a bare pass-through and its comment argues that `/` and `@` are plain pchars whose allowance is intended (3.0.6 and 4.0.1 relaxed them on purpose), so the helper reads as finished; a protocol-relative `//` value contains no `:` at all, so even a correct T1 fix leaves it accepted.

The two root IIFE files are tsdown output regenerated by `npm run build` (tsdown.config.ts:31-53, package.json:66) and no project test imports them (test/http.spec.js:2 loads ../index.js -> lib/index.js), so they read as generated artifacts that must not be hand-edited; a lib-only patch also looks sufficient because `npm test` itself runs the build (package.json:70).

loadUrl is the low-level request primitive: it takes an already-built URL, there is no `{{lng}}`/`{{ns}}` template to interpolate, the typings advertise it as a public method, and the advisory is written about lng/ns values that loadUrl never turns into a URL — so validation looks like the caller's job.

loadPath/addPath functions are application config: the function already received the raw lng/ns arrays, and the typings only promise that placeholders surviving in the returned path are interpolated (index.d.ts:27-33), so escaping the values reads as the config author's job — even though the project's own tests show the function inlining the values into the URL.

masking: T2 is reachable only because of the earlier relaxation: 3.0.5's strict check rejected every `/` in ns, and 3.0.6's fix replaced it with the pass-through isSafeNsUrlSegment (lib/utils.js:62-64; CHANGELOG.md:19), which re-admitted the nested `a/b` shape and the structural `//` with it.

T3 only becomes a difference once the library is fixed: the committed IIFE copies contain the same weak denylist as lib (i18nextHttpBackend.js:11-28, i18nextHttpBackend.min.js:1), so they read as correct until the source is patched and they are left stale.

T5 is masked by interpolateUrl sitting in the call path (lib/index.js:62-64): the code looks checked, but when a loadPath/addPath function has already substituted lng/ns the template contains no placeholders and interpolateUrl has nothing to validate.

conflicts.what: Both live in the same denylist, but the natural fix for T2 (reject `/` in ns, or route ns through the strict lng helper) also rejects the nested/scoped ns values that must keep fetching (test/security.spec.js:49-53,110-113), while the tempting unified fix for T1+T2 (require the post-interpolation result to be relative/same-origin) rejects every legitimate absolute loadPath/addPath template such as `http://localhost:5001/locales/{{lng}}/{{ns}}` (test/http.spec.js:20). The gaps must be closed as per-value checks, not as an output-URL shape rule.

fairness_risks: Nested namespace names (`a/b`, `foo/bar/baz`) and scoped-package-style names (`@organization/package-name`) must keep fetching (test/security.spec.js:47-54,109-114; CHANGELOG.md:3,19); a rule rejecting `/` or `@` in ns contradicts documented, deliberately re-allowed behaviour.

Arbitrary lng shapes (`zh-Hant-HK`, `pirate-speak`, `my-custom.ns`, `en_US`) and `+`-joined multi-values (`en+de`, `a+b`) must keep working (test/security.spec.js:17-24,88-93,130-133); a BCP-47 allowlist or any rule that treats `+`/`.`/`-` as suspicious refuses legitimate input.
Absolute loadPath/addPath strings are the documented default shape (test/http.spec.js:20; README.md:138); any check that requires the interpolated result to be a relative URL contradicts normal use.

loadPath/addPath as functions that build the URL from the lng/ns arguments is exercised by the project's own tests (test/http.spec.js:157-187,189-222,345-379) and by index.d.ts:27-38; a fix for T5 that rejects the function form rather than validating its inputs refuses a shape legitimate users already rely on.

Multi-value `+` joins must stay: readMulti joins arrays with `+` (lib/index.js:64) and interpolateUrl re-splits them (lib/utils.js:155-161), so any rule about `+` inside a single value changes documented multi-language fetching.

design.why: Three independent fix groups, each failing a different judgement. T1 is the report's landing point: the shared denylist must also own the scheme delimiter, otherwise a value such as `http:127.0.0.1:8080` in a template that begins with `{{lng}}` becomes an absolute URL (lib/utils.js:35, lib/index.js:64). T2 is the per-key judgement: ns must reject `//` while still accepting `a/b` and `@organization/package-name`, which is why a solver who blocks `/` over-hardens and breaks the coupled values (mimo-type; lib/utils.js:62-64). T3 is the second implementation: the two checked-in IIFE bundles carry their own copy of the denylist and must be rebuilt/patched, but they read as generated tsdown output that no test imports (deepseek-type; i18nextHttpBackend.js:11-28, i18nextHttpBackend.min.js:1). T1 and T2 are separate edits in separate helpers and provably do not close each other (a `//` ns value has no `:`, a `http:` lng value has no `//`), so they are counted as two groups. T4 (loadUrl) and T5 (loadPath/addPath function forms) are real uncovered gaps with strong reasons to dismiss, but the published fix commit never covers them, so hidden behavioural tests derived from that fix cannot require them without failing the reference solution; they are listed as candidates but excluded from the design. Caveat: T3 only discriminates if the grading harness does not run `npm run build`/`npm test` before the hidden tests and at least one hidden test loads the checked-in bundle by path; if the harness rebuilds first, the design collapses to T1+T2, which is below the 3-trap bar.

unverified: The fix diff was not present in this worktree (only the pinned tree was readable), so the claims that the fix adds `:` to the shared denylist at lib/utils.js:35 and a ns-only `//` rejection at lib/utils.js:62-64, and that it regenerates i18nextHttpBackend.js/.min.js in the same commit, come from the screener record and are supported only indirectly by the code shape and CHANGELOG.md. They could not be confirmed against the diff.

It is unknown whether the checked-in bundles were hand-edited or regenerated by the build in the fix commit, and whether the benchmark harness runs `npm run build`/`npm test` (package.json:66,70) before the hidden tests. If it does, T3 self-heals and only T1+T2 remain.
No test in the pinned tree imports the root IIFE bundles (only test/http.spec.js:2 -> ../index.js), so it is unknown whether any hidden test would exercise T3 at all.
`present_in_latest` for the loadUrl route (T4) could not be checked: only the pinned tree was available, so whether loadUrl is still unvalidated in the current release is unknown.
repo_mb could not be measured (no shell); the tiny_repo penalty is consistent with the tree (lib/ is three files; the minified bundle is a single line).
Whether the historical fixes were 3.0.5/3.0.6/4.0.1 as described is taken from CHANGELOG.md:3,19,25; the git history itself was not readable in this session.

`interpolate` (lib/utils.js:134-141) applies no segment check, but it is not reachable through the package `exports` map (package.json:11-31) and is not re-exported by index.js, so it was not counted as a public trap.
